title: Mira's Lord
hook: a song closes by saying whose it is: the women who signed their own names, and the names they signed
carry: in bhakti, the song belongs to god

segments.voice: Yesterday: where dharma is, there is victory. Gandhari's line, Shakuntala's witnesses, and the women of the epics given words at the hardest hour.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar. Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the one who lifted the mountain. That phrase closes song after song sung in Mirabai's name, like a stamp pressed into wax. Singers call it a chhap. Yesterday's women were given their words by the poets of the epics. The next stretch of the year turned to women whose own words survive, in songs and in a few lines of scripture, sometimes with their names pressed right into them.
screen: `MIRA'S LORD IS GIRIDHAR.` → `A STAMP PRESSED INTO WAX.` → `WOMEN IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: This is bhakti, the path of loving devotion, in the words of women who lived it. In bhakti, God isn't an idea to be proved. God is someone you love, by a name you choose and keep repeating. So start with the names they gave their God. Mira's songs end on Giridhar. Akka Mahadevi, in Karnataka, closes her vachanas on the lord white as jasmine. Andal, in Tamil, dreams her whole wedding to the Lord, verse by verse. Then the names they gave themselves. Karaikkal Ammaiyar's tradition says Shiva called her Mother. But in her own hymns she signs as a pey, a ghoul of the cremation ground, dancing near him in the night. She didn't hide the bones. She signed with them. Lal Ded, in Kashmir, let people curse her and others bring her flowers, and said neither could touch her. And some women left questions instead of songs, kept in an Upanishad. Gargi asks Yajnavalkya what the world is woven on, and when she's told to stop, she comes back later with two more. Maitreyi, offered property, asks what she'd do with something that can't make her immortal. One honest turn. With songs that traveled mouth to mouth, nobody can always say which lines go back to the woman herself. Either way, the signature keeps working. Whoever sings a Mira bhajan at a home shrine today steps aside at the end: not my Lord, but Mira's Lord. Many devotees put it this way: you borrow a saint's love for God, until one morning it's your own.
screen: `BHAKTI: GOD, LOVED BY NAME.` · `THE NAMES THEY GAVE THEIR GOD.` · `THE NAMES THEY GAVE THEMSELVES.` · `THE SINGER STEPS ASIDE.` · then, large: `NOT MY LORD, BUT MIRA'S LORD.`

segments.voice: Choose one name for God that you love, or one these women used: Giridhar, Krishna, Shiva, the Lord. Say it silently on each out-breath, the way a bhakti song comes back to the name at its close. When the mind wanders, come back to the name, without scolding yourself. If you don't pray, rest on a word that means love to you, or simply on the breath.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the women in their own words, and the names they signed. Today's word.
Your line: in bhakti, the song belongs to God. The name at the end tells you whose it is. Rest well.

howItsDone: The songs of women saints such as Mirabai, Andal and Akka Mahadevi are still sung in homes, temples and gatherings, and some Sri Vaishnava families sing Andal's wedding song at their own weddings.

fork.setup: you're Mirabai in Vrindavan. you ask to meet a holy man, and word comes back: he has vowed not to see women. what do you send back?
options: an angry letter about his vow.
one sentence: I thought there was only one man in Vrindavan, Krishna.
fork.reveal: in the story, Mira says she thought Krishna was the only man in Vrindavan, and the renunciant comes out to meet her. it's told about her, not recorded at the door.

chat.meaning: Mira's songs close with her chhap: Mira's Lord is Giridhar. In bhakti the singer steps aside and joins a saint's love for God.

tie.story: Mirabai sealed her songs to Krishna with her own name: Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the one who lifted the mountain.
tie.friend: Priya can hear Nani each morning stepping aside, loving Krishna in Mira's words until they're her own.
tie.you: whose words do you borrow when your own don't come?

chhap.meaning: a song's closing signature, telling you whose it is

Giridhar.meaning: Krishna as the one who lifted the mountain

vachanas.meaning: short devotional poems, like Akka Mahadevi's

Gargi.meaning: a woman in an Upanishad who questioned Yajnavalkya

Maitreyi.meaning: a woman in an Upanishad who asked for what can't die

bhakti.meaning: loving devotion to God, by name

sources.ref: Songs attributed to Mirabai (the closing line 'Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar')
Vachanas of Akka Mahadevi (the signature 'lord white as jasmine', Chennamallikarjuna)
Karaikkal Ammaiyar, Tiruvalankattu Mutta Tiruppatikam (closing signature); Periya Puranam (her life)
Lal Ded's vakh on praise and blame

notes: Summit sit, revisiting the poet-saints and 'in their own words where they exist' (1353–1369). Recaps follow the year's own scripts: Mirabai 1357–1358, Akka 1362, Andal 1355, Lal Ded 1365, Gargi 1367, Maitreyi 1368, Karaikkal Ammaiyar 1369.
The opening line 'Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar' is a transliteration, not an English translation; it is the signature line as given on 1358. Confirm transliteration.
Akka's 'lord white as jasmine' (Chennamallikarjuna) described as the name that closes her vachanas; confirm 'closes' is fair for her ankita.
Karaikkal Ammaiyar's signature as the pey of Karaikkal follows 1369; the specific patikam named in sources should be confirmed.
The fork's Mira and the renunciant is a story told about her (1357), not a recorded event; the reveal says so. The renunciant is sometimes named as Jiva Goswami; not named here.
Original: छाप (chhāp), Hindi; confirm spelling and pronunciation guide.
